newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - New Zealand turns popcorn into fashion.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New Zealand turns popcorn into fashion.

text.p: It's a fashion extravaganza like no other.
A rugby team plays in slow motion under laser lights, while a fashion model struts a 200 metre (yard) catwalk wearing popcorn-filled plastic boxes.
From sausage skins to compact discs, acupuncture needles to oranges, no material is too bizarre to be transformed into a wearable work of art at the annual awards in the New Zealand town of Nelson.
Each year, artists from around the world combine fashion and art, creating garments which feature in the two-hour parade incorporating theatrical performance and special effects.

This year's event, held last weekend, attracted some 245 entries from as far afield as England, Ireland, France, the Netherlands and Australia, competing in nine categories with themes ranging from bizarre bras to renaissance weddings.
It all stems from the vision of one woman, Nelson sculptor Suzie Moncrieff.
"I decided to take art off the wall and put it on the body in a moveable art exhibition," says Moncrieff, creator, producer and director of the event she initiated nine years ago.
Originally held in a field on borrowed church pews, the wearable arts have become a NZ$1 million (US$700,000) international event put together by 600 locals -- mainly volunteers who do it for love.

Parts of the show toured Singapore in July this year. The performance in an exclusive nightclub shattered perceptions of New Zealand as a country of sheep and mountains, according to the vibrant Moncrieff.
"When the show started and the first garments came out there was stunned silence. Then five minutes into it they started letting go, stamping their feet, clapping and shouting for more."
Afterwards the nightclub manager said the show was unlike anything ever seen in Singapore and made a recent show by flamboyant French designer Jean-Paul Gaultier pale in comparison.
"So move over Jean-Paul, here comes wearable art," laughs Moncrieff.
No material is too lowly to be elevated into an artwork. Coffee filters, toilet paper, moss and vacuum cleaners have all been transformed by an inspired vision.
Sometimes the artists' creation crosses over into the weird.

"Tons of strange stuff comes in. Once there was a piece made out of salmon skins and it stank. We had a garment totally created from frozen vegetables, which we kept in a freezer. You should have seen the poor model," recounts Heather Palmer, Moncrieff's sister and co-producer.
Another year, an outfit was made of huge pieces of liquorice -- a favourite with children who were later found devouring it.

This year's winning creation was a three metre (nine-foot) dragonfish designed from silk, cane and fish baskets from Fiji. Dutch artist Marianne Smits was second with a garment covered in her children's Barbie dolls.

"I went to the show last year and showed Marianne pictures of it. She was very excited as she had experimented in making human-size art and wanted to send an entry," says Philip Verstraaten, who sponsored the sending over of Smits design.
"Artists in the Netherlands were amazed. Holland has such a depth of history in art and they had never thought of holding such an event."
It all takes place in sleepy Nelson, renowned as an artistic mecca despite having barely 40,000 inhabitants.
"All the nooks and crannies of Nelson are filled with people creating something," says local personality, coffeeshop owner, prizegiver and Dutch expatriate Eelco Boswijk.
Nelson holds a week-long arts festival in celebration of the awards. From Bolivian musicians to Maori limestone sculptors. each street corner presents a unique sight.
And Moncrieff wants it to keep on growing.
"We want to increase the international aspect of the wearable arts. It would be hugely amazing if we could have the whole world coming to Nelson for this creative explosion."
